standard.title: Investigate conventions and meaning
standard.description: investigate ways that visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials are manipulated to represent ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in artworks created across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify how artists use visual conventions and materials to communicate ideas (AC9AVA6E01). They have not yet investigated how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape these choices or analysed how the same subject is represented differently across cultures and times.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate how visual conventions, processes and materials are manipulated to represent ideas, perspectives and meaning across cultures, times, places and contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying visual conventions and their purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific visual conventions used in an artwork and describe what role they play in communicating ideas or meaning
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two visual conventions in a given artwork and describe what each contributes to the meaning or effect
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a range of artworks to identify visual conventions and explain how each has been manipulated to communicate specific ideas or perspectives
wider: Compare how two artists working in different media use the same visual convention (e.g. line, colour, composition) to achieve different expressive effects
Investigate how a visual convention carries different meanings in different cultural contexts — e.g. how white is used in Western vs East Asian funerary traditions
Analyse how a First Nations Australian artist uses visual conventions that carry cultural knowledge — investigate what those conventions mean within their cultural context

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of visual convention examples before they can analyse how manipulation of conventions produces meaning. Exposure to multiple artworks, media and cultural contexts builds the visual literacy needed for genuine analysis rather than surface description.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two visual conventions in a given artwork
Describes what role each convention plays in communicating meaning — not just names the convention
Does not confuse describing what an artwork looks like with explaining how it makes meaning

nodes.label: Investigating across cultures and contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how visual conventions and processes are shaped by cultural, historical and contextual factors and explain how these factors influence meaning-making
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate one artist whose practice is shaped by cultural or historical context; explain how that context influences their use of visual conventions
nodes.typical_width: Investigate artists from at least two different cultural or historical contexts who represent a similar subject or theme; explain how context shapes their approach to visual conventions and meaning
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian artworks that cross multiple artforms — analyse how visual, performative and musical elements combine to produce layered meaning
Research the reciprocal influence between Australian and Asian artists; analyse how cross-cultural exchange shapes visual conventions and practice
Investigate how artists across different times have represented the same subject (e.g. portraiture, the natural world) — analyse what changes and what persists across cultural conventions

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe what an artist does without connecting it to cultural or historical context — the analysis stays at the surface of visual features. Investigating artists from multiple cultural and historical contexts forces students to develop the contextual reasoning habit rather than applying one familiar analytical frame.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The cross-cultural exchange direction — particularly the First Nations multimodal artworks and Australian-Asian reciprocal influence — opens genuinely rich analytical territory for advancing students. These cases require students to reason about how cultural context shapes not just what is depicted but how visual language itself operates differently.
success_criteria: Investigates at least one artist whose practice is shaped by cultural or historical context
Explains how the context influences specific visual convention or process choices
Goes beyond surface description to explain the relationship between context and meaning

nodes.label: Connecting investigation to own practice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use their investigation of other artists' use of visual conventions to inform decisions in their own visual arts practice
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one specific insight from investigating other artists' use of visual conventions that has influenced a decision in own work; explain the connection
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how investigating artists' choices informs own approach to visual conventions and processes; document specific points of influence and how they are adapted, not just imitated
wider: Develop written accounts (catalogue entries, reviews or discussions) that connect the investigation of other artists to own artistic decisions
Investigate how artists are inspired by practitioners from other countries or cultures and use this as a model for own cross-cultural investigation
Construct an argument about why investigating diverse artistic traditions produces stronger and more distinctive own practice than studying a single tradition

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together visual convention analysis (Node 1) and cultural/contextual investigation (Node 2) and connect both to their own practice decisions. The integration is the learning — students who can analyse other artists but cannot use that analysis to inform their own work have not reached this standard's demand.

Students commonly describe what they have investigated without articulating the connection to own practice — 'I liked how Mondrian used primary colours' without reasoning through how that insight changes a specific decision in own work. Scaffolding the connection explicitly (what did I learn, what decision did it change, how is my adaptation different from imitation?) builds the analytical-to-practical transfer.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one specific insight from investigating other artists that influenced own work
Explains the connection between the investigation and the decision — not just 'I was inspired by'
